paras: The attempted lynching of Seymour took place in the village of Rock Falls, Whiteside County, Illinois, on the night of Monday, January 30, 1882, when twenty to thirty men went to the house of a man named Seymour intending to lynch him. Seymour and his wife were accused of beating, starving and otherwise abusing a seven-year-old girl who lived in their household, and both had fled before the men arrived. A dispatch from nearby Sterling carried the story to papers from Pennsylvania to California, most of which dwelt on the cruelty charged against the couple rather than on the lynching party.

According to a Chicago Times special reprinted in the Ottawa Free Trader, Mrs. Bolton of Rock Falls had been left with eight small children after her husband was sent to the insane asylum. About a month before the attempt, one of them, a girl of seven, went to live with the Seymours, and the Sterling dispatch said she "was working for the Seymours." On Saturday word reached her mother that the child was being abused, and on going to the house she found her "in a horrible state from beating and starvation." The girl was taken away and placed under a physician's care, and warrants were issued for the couple's arrest.

The Times special and a variant Sterling dispatch accused Seymour of confining the girl in a cellar all day without food, whipping her with a horsewhip until her body was "black and blue and sore," and tossing her toward the ceiling to let her fall to the floor.

On the day of the attempt a "great number of people" visited the child, and the Times correspondent wrote that what they saw "so maddened them" that about 10 o'clock that night twenty to thirty disguised men went to Seymour's house to lynch him. Word of their coming reached the couple, and they fled. The men searched the residence and a number of other houses without finding him, and a National Associated Press dispatch said every house in the village was searched.

The Times special closed by saying the people of the village were "determined to have the fellow puished" by whatever means would reach that result. No report of the Seymours' capture, arrest or trial was found in the coverage, which ends with the statement that a diligent search had failed to find them.

The Sterling dispatch, dated January 31, ran that day and the next under headlines aimed at the couple: "Cruel Treatment" in the Yankton Press and Daily Dakotaian, "Inhuman Treatment" in the St. Paul Daily Globe, "Human Fiends" in the Wheeling Register and "A Flendish Fair" [Fiendish Pair] in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union. Each copy of this short dispatch ended by calling the methods of cruelty "too diabolical for mention" and reported the lynching party in a single sentence without comment. A fuller variant in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, headed "Inhuman Cruelty," listed the abuse and said the villagers had made "a determined though unsuccessful attempt to lynch Seymour."

The Omaha Daily Bee printed a separate Chicago dispatch under the headline "Attempted Lynching," while the Portland Daily Press reduced the episode to one sentence about an attempt on "Mr. and Mrs. Seymour" for cruelty to "an orphan child." Closer to home, the Ottawa Free Trader in Illinois headed the Times special "Anxious to Lynch a Brute" and kept the correspondent's remark that returned Californians "said it looked like old times, and meant business." None of the reports gave the race of the Seymours, the child or the men who sought them.

The Yankton paper's text says Seymour "escaped with his life," while the Globe, the Wheeling Register and the Record-Union print "escaped with his wife" in the same sentence. Because the Lancaster, Portland and Times versions all say both husband and wife fled, the Yankton wording is probably a misprint of the same line.

bases: Twenty to thirty men went to Seymour's house at night to lynch him over the alleged abuse of a child, but he and his wife had fled and no one was harmed (A1, A20, A9).

A group of twenty to thirty men set out without legal authority to lynch Seymour over the abuse charged against him, but he escaped and no one was killed, so this was an attempted lynching only (A1, A20).

Three separately written reports, the Sterling wire (A1, A2), a National Associated Press Chicago dispatch (A8) and a Chicago Times special (A20), agree that a party went to Seymour's house to lynch him and that the couple had fled.
